title: Drive a piston into its bore through a ring compressor while the other hand holds the compressor flat on the deck
instruction: Install the piston in the bore.
context: Automotive and small-engine mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00, 49-3053.00) fit pistons this way in every engine rebuild. The rings stand out past the piston, so a ring compressor squeezes them into their grooves and the piston is driven out of the compressor into the bore. Engine manuals and rebuild guides give the rule: hold the compressor down flat and square on the deck while driving the piston, because each ring pushes the band up as it is squeezed past the band's lip, and a band that rides up even a millimeter lets that ring spring out, catch on the deck's edge and jam the piston, or break if it is driven on. One hand therefore holds the compressor down the whole time while the other drives the piston home, then both let go.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Engine block: a single-cylinder small-engine block (gray painted cast iron, 15 x 15 cm, 6 cm tall) fixed to the table, centered at x 26, y -17, its machined deck on top at z 6 with four head-bolt and two dowel holes. Its bore (68 mm, a steel liner with a 1 mm chamfer at its mouth) is vertical, axis at x 26, y -17. Piston: aluminum, 67.6 mm across and 5 cm tall, with its pin and rod 250 g, an arrow on the crown; three rings in grooves 5 mm (top compression ring), 9 mm (second ring) and 13 mm (oil ring) below the crown. It starts with its skirt in the bore and its crown 2.2 cm above the deck; it slides only along the bore's axis and seats with the crown 1 cm below the deck, where the rod's big end meets the crank journal (crank at bottom dead center, not shown). Ring compressor: pliers type, 200 g, a spring-steel band 1.8 cm tall (68.4 mm inside, rolled lip to 8 cm across) squeezing all three rings, standing on the deck around the piston; its two steel handles, locked squeezed by a ratchet bar and with red vinyl grips on their outer 9 cm, reach from 4 to 19 cm out from the bore's axis toward the robot's left, 30 degrees forward of the y axis (ends near x 35.5, y -0.5), 0.8 cm above the deck. The compressor slides only along the bore's axis; nothing holds it down but its weight. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. A ring is crossing while it is within 2.5 mm above the deck (in the band's lower lip and on the bore's 1 mm chamfer). A ring escapes if the compressor's band is more than 1 mm off the deck (a 1.2 mm-tall ring fits through the gap) while that ring is in the gap between the deck and the band, or while it crosses the deck plane, and also if it goes from above the 2.5 mm entry to below the deck within one 50 ms step (driven over 5 cm/s, it is slammed past the band's lip rather than squeezed in); an escaped ring jams the piston and scores 0, irreversible: pressing the band back down and pushing on doesn't undo it. At the end, nothing counts while a tool point is still on the work (within 21 cm of the bore's axis, which covers the 19 cm handles, and lower than 6 cm above the band's top): 0. With the hands off: 1.0 when all three rings are in the bore (each 1 mm or more below the deck, past the chamfer), the crown is within 2 mm of its seat (half the 4 mm between ring grooves) and the compressor rests on the deck within 1 mm, released and left standing empty there for the mechanic to unlock and lift off; otherwise 0.2 for each ring in cleanly (0.2, 0.4 or 0.6). Full score also needs both arms back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started and still); a finished job with the arms elsewhere scores 0.9. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, a 1 mm feeler gauge or dial indicator at the band's edge on the handle side shows any lift (or film it from the side), a look into the bore shows a broken or protruding ring, and a depth gauge measures the crown below the deck.
reset_notes: Pull the piston back up until its crown is 2.2 cm above the deck, check the three rings are whole and in their grooves (replace a broken ring), close the compressor around them and lock its handles, stand it flat on the deck with the handles pointing as described, and turn the crank to bottom dead center.
fidelity: A shop taps the crown with a hammer handle; here one hand pushes it down steadily. Piston and rod are one slide on the bore's axis, the crank a stop. The compressor only slides on that axis, so tipping is modeled as lifting (the 1 mm limit applies to its whole rim). Ring forces are modeled: each crossing ring pushes the piston back with 4 N and the band up with 6 N, falling off at 600 N/m, so an unheld band rides up about 7 mm; an escaped ring holds the piston where it is.
